output:
Buy insurance and you pay a monthly premium. But when something goes wrong, the company does not simply cover everything. You pay the first slice yourself. That slice is the deductible.

Say your car insurance carries a £500 deductible. A repair bill arrives for £2,000. You hand over £500, and the insurer pays the remaining £1,500. If the damage only costs £300, you pay all of it and claim nothing.

The size of that slice is usually your choice when you sign up. Pick a high deductible and your monthly premium drops, because the insurer expects to pay out less. Pick a low one and your premium rises.

Think of a restaurant bill split with a friend who has agreed to cover anything above twenty pounds. You always pay your twenty, no matter how large the total grows.

Why does this exist? It stops people claiming for every tiny scratch, which would flood insurers with paperwork. It also keeps you a little careful, since you have money at stake too.

The trade-off matters. A high deductible saves you money each month, but it hurts badly if you need to claim unexpectedly.

In short, a deductible is the fixed amount you pay yourself before your insurer starts contributing.
